open-question.question: The mission re-evaluates every one of the 35 invariants in today's `CLAUDE.md` and compresses each to its rule, its reason, and the retired forms that must not return. May a re-evaluation end in a rule itself being dropped or changed, for example one found obsolete or one that only records an accepted limitation, or does the mission change only wording and placement, every rule standing exactly as it binds today?
open-question.alternative: No rule is dropped or changed: every one of the 35 invariants keeps binding exactly as it does today. Re-evaluation cuts only text that binds nothing (mechanics already stated in the runtime files, field measurements, dates, the history of how a form came about) and moves each rule to its home. An entry that records an accepted limitation ("accepted as it stands", "accepted as never to be changed") stays as a rule, compressed to what must not be changed and why. Candidates for retirement are not recorded anywhere. The mission's diff can be reviewed as a pure move and compression: no tool, test, runtime file, or behaviour changes, and a reviewer has only to check that every rule survives, so the risk of losing a design decision while rewriting 145,667 bytes is the lowest of any option. Rules whose subject no longer stands in the tree (the pre-split missions, the pre-flip TASKS_DONE.md note) and entries kept only to stop a limitation being "fixed" are carried into the new tree as they are, so part of the bulk the byte budgets must hold is text the re-evaluation already judged dead, and the goal's "every invariant is re-evaluated" yields nothing beyond compression.

alternative.id: Wording only, candidates kept for later

open-question.alternative: This mission changes only wording and placement, every rule binding as it does today, as in the wording-only option. Where re-evaluation finds a rule obsolete or one that only records an accepted limitation, the runner leaves the rule standing in its new home and records it as a retirement candidate, with the reason, in one draft under ideas/ for a later mission to decide. Keeps this mission's diff a pure move and compression while not wasting the judgment the re-evaluation forms: the candidates reach a later mission as a ready list, where each drop can be decided on its own with the tree already in place. The dead text still has to fit inside this mission's byte budgets, and the draft is one more document the tree must point at and the update skill must keep honest until a later mission takes it up, which nothing schedules.

alternative.id: Drop obsolete rules, decided up front

open-question.alternative: A rule may be dropped, never changed, and only when its subject no longer exists in the tree or the history it guards is closed (for example the pre-split missions and the pre-flip TASKS_DONE.md note); every other rule, accepted-limitation entries included, keeps binding exactly as today. Each drop is decided in this mission before tasks are derived, the review pass authoring one open question per candidate, so the recorded decisions list every rule that leaves. No runtime file, tool, or test changes. Removes the clearest dead weight from the tree while every drop is a recorded, revertible decision rather than a runner's call, and the rule that stops a limitation being "fixed" is left untouched, so no behaviour can drift. Adds a round of questions before derivation for a handful of small drops, and an obsolete-looking rule may still bind something (the TASKS_DONE.md note also says no runner is to read or recreate the file), so each candidate needs care that a compressed retired-forms line could have given at no cost.

alternative.id: Drop obsolete and limitation rules, decided up front

open-question.alternative: A rule may be dropped, never changed, when it is obsolete or when it only records an accepted limitation (the commit tool's exit-128 retry accepted as it stands, the hand-rendered attribute rule, markup accepted in an alternative's text, the unbounded show print); a dropped limitation entry leaves behaviour as it is and stops forbidding a later fix. Each drop is decided in this mission before tasks are derived, one open question per candidate. No runtime file, tool, or test changes. Cuts the largest class of text that binds no current behaviour, the accepted-limitation records written in the latest mission's tasks, so the tree states what the code must do rather than every fix that was weighed and declined. An accepted-limitation entry exists precisely so a later editor does not "fix" what was left on purpose; dropping it removes that guard, and a later mission may re-measure and re-decide something already settled, at a cost the drop saved only in bytes.

A rule may be dropped, never changed, when its subject no longer exists in the tree, under one criterion recorded as a decision of this mission; the task runner compressing that area applies it and names each dropped rule, with its reason, in its task's verified bar. Accepted-limitation entries and every other rule keep binding as today. No runtime file, tool, or test changes. Removes dead rules without a question round before derivation, since applying one narrow, checkable criterion (the subject is gone from the tree) is a runner's job, and every drop still shows in a commit body and its diff. A design decision leaves the project's record by a runner's judgment rather than a recorded answer, and a runner reading "subject gone" loosely can drop a rule that still binds (a retired form that must not return is exactly a rule whose subject is gone); how much is left to runners also depends on the axis the Placement decision timing question owns.

alternative.id: Drop or change rules, docs only

open-question.alternative: Re-evaluation may drop a rule (obsolete or limitation-only) or change what it binds, narrowing, loosening, or merging rules where it finds one wrong or redundant, but only where the change needs no edit to a runtime file, tool, test, or build: the rules change what a later editor may do, never what the code does now. Each drop or change is decided in this mission before tasks are derived, one open question per rule. Gives the re-evaluation its full value at the level of the rules themselves, so overlapping or contradictory invariants written over many missions can be reconciled into a smaller, coherent set rather than faithfully compressed, while the plugin's behaviour stays exactly as shipped. Many questions may be raised across 35 rules before derivation, lengthening the mission's preparation, and a rule changed without touching the code it governs can leave code that the new rule no longer explains or that now contradicts it until a later mission aligns them.

alternative.id: Drop or change rules with the code

open-question.alternative: Re-evaluation may drop or change any rule, and a changed rule carries the change to the runtime files, tools, tests, and rebuilt host trees it governs in this mission, so rule and code stay in step. Each drop or change is decided in this mission before tasks are derived, one open question per rule. Every rule in the new tree states exactly what the code does, with no rule left wrong or out of step, and a defect the re-evaluation exposes is fixed where it is found rather than deferred. Turns a documentation mission into a plugin-behaviour mission of unbounded size across all of core/ and the host trees, overlapping the defined mission_project-defined-knowledge-placement/ that changes the context-reading runners and finish, and mixes behaviour changes into a diff that is otherwise reviewable as moves and compression.

open-question.question: Most of the 35 invariants in today's `CLAUDE.md` govern files under `core/` (the six tools, the shared procedures, the skills, the agents), yet `core/` can hold no node: the host build stops on any file at its top level and renders every file under its four directories into every host tree, and a standing rule keeps editor-facing prose and rationale out of those rendered files, tool sources included. The goal has the parent node, the small root, describe `core/`. Where do the compressed rules governing files under `core/` live: in the root itself, in a file outside `core/` that the root points at, inside the governed files with the rule against rationale in runtime files lifted in whole or for the tool sources only, or in a file under `core/` that the build is changed to leave unrendered?
open-question.recommendation: It is the one option that keeps every core rule in a README.md node inside the folder it governs, split four ways so each stays within a node's budget, with no rationale in any rendered file and no build code changed: the per-host exclude key already exists and is empty in all three definitions, a forgotten entry shows as a new file in the committed host tree, and the build's host-name and old-word scans, which still read these files, only hold them to the layer's own wording rules.
open-question.alternative: The compressed rules are split by subfolder into a `README.md` in each of `core/tools/`, `core/shared/`, `core/skills/`, and `core/agents/`, each kept out of every host tree by listing it in the existing per-host `exclude` key of every `scripts/hosts/<host>/settings.toml`, with no change to the build's Python; the root describes `core/` and points at each, and the rule against rationale stays in force for every rendered file. Each rule stands inside the very folder it governs under the `README.md` name the rest of the tree uses, found by anyone browsing that folder, using a build mechanism that already exists, so no build code changes and no rendered file carries rationale. Every host definition must carry the same four exclusions, so a host added or a `README.md` forgotten in one `exclude` list silently ships the rationale into that host's tree with no check catching it; the nodes also stand in folders the goal treats as rendered and described by their parent, and the rules spanning subfolders still need a home, which depends on how the question on rules spanning folders settles.

Every compressed rule governing files under `core/` stands in the root `CLAUDE.md` itself, beside the root's description of `core/` and its subfolders; no other file holds them, the build and every host's settings stay as they are, and the rule keeping rationale out of rendered runtime files, tool sources included, stands unchanged. Nothing new is created and nothing about the build or the runtime rule changes: the rules sit in the one file every host already loads as project instructions, so an editor working anywhere in `core/` has them in front of them without following any pointer. Most of the 35 invariants govern `core/`, so even compressed they put the bulk of today's rule text back into the root, the file the mission exists to make small and that grew back from 22,329 bytes after the last hand compression; whether this fits at all depends on the root limit the byte-budget question sets.

The compressed `core/` rules live in one dedicated document at a path outside `core/` and `hosts/`, which the build never reads or renders, and the root's description of `core/` carries a pointer to it with a when-to-follow note; nothing under `core/` changes, no host's settings change, and the rule against rationale in runtime files stands in whole. Keeps the root small and the runtime rule and build untouched while giving every `core/` rule one findable home, read only by someone about to edit `core/`, so no runner or published host tree ever carries the rationale. The rules sit away from the files they govern, reached only by an editor who follows the root's pointer, and the document is a node that is not a `README.md` in the folder it describes, so the pointer, covered-folder, and byte-budget checks must know it by name; one file holding every `core/` rule may itself grow past a node's limit, and if its path falls under `docs/` its fate is tied to what the docs-role question decides that folder serves.

alternative.id: One file per core folder outside core

open-question.alternative: The compressed `core/` rules are split by the subfolder they govern into separate documents outside `core/` and `hosts/`, one each for `core/tools/`, `core/shared/`, `core/skills/`, and `core/agents/`, each pointed at from the root's description of that subfolder; the build, the host settings, and the runtime rule stay unchanged. Each document stays small and is read only by someone working in the one subfolder it covers, so the rules scale with `core/` without any single file or the root growing large, and no rendered file carries rationale. Four documents mirror `core/`'s structure from somewhere else, so a subfolder added or renamed leaves its document stale with nothing tying the two together, and the many rules reaching across tools, procedures, skills, and agents (committing, shell commands, the return contracts) need a home among them, which depends on how the question on rules spanning folders settles.

The rule keeping editor-facing prose and rationale out of runtime files is lifted in whole: each compressed rule is written into the file it governs, a tool's module docstring or comments, a skill's `SKILL.md`, a shared procedure, or an agent file, and is rendered with it into every host tree; the root describes `core/` and points at no separate rule file. A rule stands exactly where the code or prose it constrains stands, so whoever edits a file reads its rule in the same view, and the rule moves, renames, and is deleted together with its file. Every runner loading a skill, procedure, or agent then reads maintainer rationale and lists of retired forms it is not meant to act on, costing context on every run and risking a runner reading "the retired form" as an instruction, and the rationale is published verbatim into every distribution repository; a rule spanning several files must be repeated in each or assigned to one of them, and the standing runtime rule and its reasons are reversed.

The rule against rationale in runtime files is lifted for the tool sources only: each rule governing one tool lives in that tool's own source, in comments or a docstring section its `--help` does not print, so no runner sees it; the rules governing the Markdown runtime files (skills, shared procedures, agents) and those spanning tools and prose live in one document outside `core/` and `hosts/`, which the root points at, and the ban stands for every Markdown runtime file. The largest rule blocks today, the missions, task-list, open-question, fold, and commit tools, move next to the code they explain, which no runner reads as prose, while the Markdown files runners do read stay free of rationale and the outside document stays much smaller than one holding every `core/` rule. The rules are split across two kinds of home with a line to draw for every rule touching both a tool and the prose that calls it, the tool sources still ship that rationale into every host tree, and the outside document carries the same not-a-`README.md` and pointer-check burden as any outside home.

As with the tool-source lift, each rule governing one tool lives in that tool's own source in comments or a docstring section `--help` does not print, and the ban stands for every Markdown runtime file; the rules governing the skills, shared procedures, and agents, and those spanning tools and prose, stand in the root `CLAUDE.md` itself, so no new document is created. No new document and no pointer to resolve: the per-tool rules sit beside their code and the rest sit in the one file every host loads, so an editor of any `core/` file meets its rules either in the file or in the root. The non-tool `core/` rules (committing, shell commands, the return contracts, the annotating passes, the answer sweep) remain a large share of today's invariants, so the root still grows well past a small root, which holds only if the byte-budget question sets a generous root limit; the tool sources still ship their rationale into every host tree.

The compressed `core/` rules live in one document standing directly in `core/` (such as `core/README.md`), and `scripts/build_hosts.py` is changed so that this one file is accepted at the top level of `core/` rather than stopping the build with exit 2, and is left out of every host tree; the root points at it, and the rule against rationale stays in force for every rendered file. The rules sit at the head of the folder they govern, under the name a reader looks for first, while no rendered file or published tree carries them and the runtime rule stays whole. It changes the generic build, whose refusal of any top-level `core/` file is what keeps stray files out of every host, to carry one named exception, and puts a non-runtime file into the directory defined as the host-neutral runtime layer, which the `host-name-in-core` scan still reads; one file holding every `core/` rule may outgrow a node's byte limit.

open-question.question: The mission adds a maintainer-only skill under `.claude/skills/` that, beside a pytest check of pointers, covered folders, and byte budgets, keeps the tree of `README.md` nodes below the root `CLAUDE.md` honest. What does one run of that skill do: repair only what the check reports, compare every node with the folder it describes and rewrite what has gone stale, bring the nodes up to date with the commits made since its last run, or re-compress nodes that have grown?
open-question.recommendation: Commits are how a node falls behind its folder, so the run reads exactly the commits made since its last one from an anchor in the log, the pattern the starting-state refresh already uses, keeps every still-true sentence byte-identical so its diff is the change in the ground and nothing else, and costs what changed instead of a read of the whole repository, with the check's failures repaired in the same run.
open-question.alternative: Work found by: the commits made since the skill's last run, the anchor being the latest commit under the skill's own subject marker found in the log (the pattern the missions tool's `since` uses for the starting state), plus the check's failures; with no anchor, the first run compares every node with its folder. Edits: updates, in place, the nodes of the folders those commits changed and the pointer notes above them, keeping every still-true sentence byte-identical, and repairs every check failure. Re-compression: only as far as a budget failure forces it. Action: writes and commits under its marker, which moves the anchor. Each run's cost follows the change rather than the size of the tree, and its diff is the change in the ground and nothing else, the same reasons the starting state is refreshed from an anchor rather than re-explored, so the skill can be run often without re-reading the whole repository. It sees only drift a commit path points at: a node wrong from the start, one made wrong by a commit to a different folder (a root rule changed by a tool commit), or drift that predates the anchor stays until a full comparison; and a run that changes nothing lands no commit, so the anchor does not move and every later run re-reads the same window. How much drift reaches the nodes between runs depends on the placement-mission question, whether finish writes lasting changes into the nodes itself.

Work found by: the pytest check alone; the skill runs it and takes its failures as the whole worklist. Edits: repairs exactly what the check reports, a broken pointer fixed, a missing node written for an uncovered folder, an over-budget root, node, or note cut until it passes, and nothing else. Re-compression: only as far as a budget failure forces it. Staleness of content the check cannot see: not looked for. Action: writes the repairs and commits them. The run is bounded and repeatable: its worklist is the check's own print, so two runs on the same tree do the same thing, a clean check means a no-op run with no diff, and the skill stays a short file rather than another release-skill-sized procedure. Everything the check cannot measure drifts unseen, which is the drift the tree is there to prevent: a node describing files that moved, a rule a later task changed, or an entry naming one of two files (today's `ideas/` entry names `benchmark.md` and not `kepala.md`) all pass a pointer, coverage, and byte check, so the skill keeps the tree resolvable and small rather than true. How much a budget failure forces it to cut depends on the limits the byte-budget question sets.

Work found by: the pytest check plus each node's size against the size it had after the skill's last run (or a margin below its budget). Edits: repairs every check failure as in a check-only run, and re-compresses every node or note that has grown past that mark, back to its rule, reason, and retired forms, without comparing it with its folder. Staleness of content: not looked for. Action: writes and commits. It targets the failure already seen in this file's history: the hand compression of `05815f18` to 22,329 bytes grew back to 171,838, mostly through task commits (105 of the 157 that changed it), so cutting growth back before the budget is hit keeps headroom for every later addition instead of waiting for the check to fail. Re-compressing a node whose facts still hold rewrites true text into different prose, a diff that records no change in the folder and can drop a reason or a retired form a later reader needed; and like a check-only run it never notices a node that is short but wrong. The growth mark depends on the limits the byte-budget question sets.

Work found by: the commits since the skill's last run, anchored on its own subject marker as above, plus the check's failures and each touched node's growth since the last run; with no anchor, a full comparison. Edits: updates the nodes of the changed folders in place, repairs every check failure, and re-compresses each node it touched, or found grown past its mark, back to rule, reason, and retired forms. Action: writes and commits under its marker. It covers both ways the old file decayed, facts falling behind the code and text piling up, while keeping each run's reading proportional to what changed since the last one. It carries the incremental run's blind spots (drift no commit path points at, an anchor that a no-op run does not move) and adds re-compression's churn on the nodes it touches, so a node edited for one fact may come back with every sentence reworded, a larger diff to review per run. The growth mark depends on the byte-budget question's limits.

Work found by: comparing every node, the root included, with the current contents of the folder it describes, every run, plus the check's failures. Edits: rewrites in place whatever no longer holds and adds what is missing, keeping every still-true sentence byte-identical, and repairs every check failure. Re-compression: only as far as a budget failure forces it. Action: writes and commits. It catches drift however it arose, a hand commit, a merge, a node wrong from the day it was written, or a change in one folder that falsifies a rule stated in another, because it measures each node against the tree rather than against a log, and it needs no anchor or marker. Every run reads the whole repository, a cost that grows with the tree (nearly 500 tracked files today) and makes the skill expensive to run often; and a model re-reading an unchanged folder tends to write different prose for the same facts, so the byte-identical rule must hold firmly or each run produces noise diffs. What every node means depends on the covered-folder question, and how mechanically a node can be compared depends on the node-structure question.

Work found by: comparing every node with its folder every run, plus the check's failures and each node's growth. Edits: rewrites what is stale, adds what is missing, repairs every check failure, and re-compresses every node that has grown past its mark back to rule, reason, and retired forms. Action: writes and commits. It is the most complete single run: after it, every node is true to its folder, passes the check, and has its headroom restored, so a maintainer needs no second kind of run and the tree is reset to its intended shape each time. It is the costliest run, reading the whole repository and rewriting every grown node, with the largest diff to review and the most chances to drop a reason or a retired form in compression; run rarely because of that cost, it lets drift accumulate between runs. The growth mark depends on the byte-budget question's limits.

Work found by: comparing every node with its folder, plus the check's failures and each node's growth. Edits: none; the run prints the stale, missing, failing, and overgrown items it found, each with its node and what it found, and writes and commits nothing, the maintainer fixing them by hand or as tasks of a mission. No run can rewrite a rule wrongly or compress away a reason unseen, since every change to a node passes through a person or a reviewed task, and the skill itself stays read-only and cheap to trust. The tree stays honest only as far as someone acts on each report, the step that failed before, when nothing kept the old file in line and it grew back; and a run that commits nothing leaves no marker in the log, so it cannot run from an anchor and must read the whole repository every time.

Work found by and edits: whichever of the jobs above the maintainer names as the run's argument, check repair, an update from the commits since the last run, a full comparison, or re-compression, with one of them fixed as the default when no argument is given. Action: writes and commits under one subject marker whatever the job, so the incremental job's anchor is the latest run of any kind. One skill serves both a quick routine pass and an occasional deep one, so the maintainer pays for a full comparison or a re-compression only when it is wanted, while the cheap job runs often. The skill carries every job's procedure, the largest file of the alternatives and several paths to keep consistent, and which job runs becomes a per-run judgment: a default that is the cheap job lets the deep jobs be skipped indefinitely, and the drift each job misses persists until someone chooses another.

open-question.question: The mission's pytest check holds the root `CLAUDE.md`, every `README.md` node below it, and each pointer's when-to-follow note within a byte budget, and the three limits constrain one another, since the root carries one pointer with its note for each of the thirteen tracked top-level folders beside its other contents and a node carries the pointers to what lies below it. Today's root is 171,838 bytes, and an earlier hand compression to 22,329 bytes grew back. What are the three byte limits: for the root, for a node, and for a note?
open-question.recommendation: Three plain numbers with no exception table to creep upward: the root limit sits at a size already shown to hold the whole repository's guidance in compressed form, so it is meetable with the root still describing the folders whose README name is taken, a 12,000-byte node holds a folder's compressed rules, and the check still cuts today's root by about nine tenths and holds it there by test.
open-question.alternative: Three fixed numbers, each applying uniformly: the root at most 20,000 bytes, every node at most 12,000 bytes, and every note at most 400 bytes, two or three short sentences. Notes count inside the size of the file holding them, so the root's thirteen pointers take at most about 5,200 bytes, and the root total sits just under the 22,329 bytes of the earlier hand compression, which held the same eight sections with 23 invariant bullets. The root limit is close to a size already shown to hold the whole repository's guidance in compressed form, so it is very likely meetable whatever the sibling placement questions settle, while still cutting today's 171,838-byte root by about nine tenths and holding it there by test rather than by hand. A 20,000-byte root is large enough to keep many folder-specific rules in the root rather than in the nodes where someone working there would find them, so the budget does less to push knowledge down the tree; whether 12,000 bytes suffices for the largest folders still depends on the sibling questions on node structure and covered folders.

Three fixed numbers, each applying uniformly: the root `CLAUDE.md` at most 10,000 bytes, every `README.md` node at most 6,000 bytes, and every when-to-follow note at most 200 bytes, about one line. The note limit is counted inside the root's and each node's own size, so the root's thirteen top-level pointers take at most about 2,600 bytes of note text and leave the rest for what the repo is, the rules binding everywhere, the knowledge-placement rules, the description of `core/`, `hosts/`, and `gurita-vscode/`, and the 623-byte `## Mission Workflow` section. The limits sit well below the 22,329-byte form that grew back, so the tree cannot drift toward a large root a little at a time, and every rule has to be compressed to its rule, reason, and retired forms rather than carried over with its mechanics and history. The root also has to describe `core/`, `hosts/`, and `gurita-vscode/`, whose names are taken, and a 6,000-byte node leaves little room in folders of many files such as `tests/` (72 files outside the fixtures) or `gurita-vscode/src/` (87), so the limits may be unmeetable depending on where the core rules live, what a node's structure requires (an entry per file, for one), and whether root-level files get entries in the root, all owned by sibling questions; a limit hit by honest content invites cutting a reason rather than moving it.

Three fixed numbers set as regression guards rather than compression targets: the root and every node at most 40,000 bytes, the size at which Claude Code warns that a large `CLAUDE.md` affects performance, and every note at most 1,000 bytes. The actual compression is left to the tasks and the update skill, the check only stopping a file from growing past the ceiling. The limits are anchored to an outside threshold rather than chosen arbitrarily, so they never force a sound rule out of the file it belongs in, and no task fails merely because honest content ran a few hundred bytes over a guessed number. A root of up to 40,000 bytes is almost twice the form that grew back, so the budget gives no pressure toward a small root and the tree could regrow to a size the goal calls replacing; the warning threshold is a host behaviour no `settings.toml` records, so it is unverified here and may change, and a note of 1,000 bytes is a paragraph, not a when-to-follow note.

The root's and each node's limit covers its own body only, the pointer lines and their notes excluded and bounded separately: the root body at most 10,000 bytes, a node body at most 8,000 bytes, and each note at most 300 bytes, so the root's total grows by at most one note's allowance per pointer as top-level folders are added, about 3,900 bytes for today's thirteen. The check finds the pointers it already resolves and subtracts them before measuring the body. It removes the coupling the question names: adding a folder or a pointer never squeezes the rules standing beside them, so the root's and each node's rule budget stays fixed however many children it points at. No total size of the root is bounded, so a project growing folders grows the root without the check noticing, and the check has to tell pointer lines from body text exactly, which depends on the pointer form a sibling question owns; the limits are harder to state and to read off a file than one size per file.

The root at most 16,000 bytes, each note at most 300 bytes, and every node at most 8,000 bytes by default, with a short table kept in the check giving a larger limit, up to 16,000 bytes, to named nodes whose folders hold many files (for example `tests/` or `gurita-vscode/src/`). Every other node takes the default. It fits the repository's uneven folders, where the largest hold over seventy files and the smallest one, without either loosening every node to the largest folder's size or forcing the largest folders to drop what someone working there needs. The exception table is the growth path the earlier compression lost to: each time a node runs over, raising or adding its exception is one line in a test, so limits can creep upward with each change; which nodes need an exception at all depends on the sibling questions on node structure and covered folders.

No numbers are fixed now: the task that writes the check sets three uniform limits from the finished tree, each at the measured size plus a fixed margin of 10 percent, the root's own size, the largest node's, and the longest note's, and records them in the check. The limits are grounded in content that has actually been compressed and placed, so none is unmeetable or so loose it does nothing, and the mutual constraint between root, node, and note is satisfied by construction. The budget follows the content instead of shaping it, so the compression has no target while it is done and the largest node or the root sets the limit for everything; the decision of how small the tree must be is moved to a runner completing a task rather than made in this mission's decisions.

No uniform node limit: the check holds one table giving the root and every node its own limit, each set at that file's size when the tree is finished plus a margin of 10 percent, and every note at most 300 bytes; a new node takes a default of 8,000 bytes until its own entry is added, and a limit is raised only by editing its entry in the table. Every file is held near the size it was compressed to, so growth in any one file, the root included, is stopped at once and any raise is a visible line in a diff that a reviewer can question. The table needs an entry per node and changes whenever one is added, removed, or legitimately grows, a hand-kept list the update skill must maintain; the limits record what the tree happened to be rather than a size anyone chose, so a file compressed poorly at the start is held at its poor size.
